la:adj:morus.html:
mōrus, a, um, adj., = μωρός,
foolish, silly (Plautin.).
Adj.: amor mores hominum moros et morosos facit,: ut hoc utimur more moro molestoque,.—
Subst.
mōrus, i, m., a fool, simpleton: morus es,.—
mōra, ae, f., a foolish woman, .— Hence, adv.: mōrē, foolishly (Plautin.): more hoc fit atque stulte,.

la:verb:morior.gloss: to die, be slain, fall (in battle), perish
senses: to die, be slain, fall (in battle), perish
la:verb:morior.html:
mŏrĭor, mortŭus, 3 (
fut. part. moriturus, a, um, ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; old forms acc. to the fourth conj.: si vivimu' sive morīmur, Enn. ap. P.; Ann. v. 384 Vahl.; inf. moriri, ; ; ; Ritschl N. cr.; ), v. dep.
Sanscr. root mar-, die; Gr. μορ- (μρο-, βρο-), μαρ; βροτός, μαραίνω; cf.: morbus, marceo
, to die (cf.: pereo, intereo, occĭdo, occumbo, obeo, exspiro; class.).
Lit.: vivam an moriar, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. metus, p. 123 Müll. (Trag. v. 179 Vahl.): ego cum genui, tum morituros scivi, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 361 Vahl.): mori,: atque eundem (L. Tarquinium) ... accepimus mortuum esse, cum duodequadraginta regnavisset annos,: moriendum certe est,: desiderio,of desire,: ut fame senatores quinque morerentur,: me esse homines mortuom dicant fame,; so, fame,; : fame et siti,: siti, id. 4, 30, 8; ; Pomp. ap. : vigilando,: ex vulnere, of a wound, Pollio ap. : in tormentis,: alterius amore,: curis, (6, 51): fame,: inediā,: significabat interruptis atque morientibus vocibus,dying accents, the accents of a dying man,: mori videbamus in studio dimetiundi paene caeli atque terrae C. Galum,spend his whole life in,: cum te complexā morientem, Galle, puellā Vidimus,desperately in love, dying for love,: ei mihi, si quis, Acrius ut moriar, venerit alter amor,: moriar, si, may I die, if, etc., .—
Transf., of things, to die away, decay, to wither away, pass away, to vanish, lose its strength, etc.; of members of the body: id quod supra vinculum est, moritur,loses its vitality,.—Of plants: rutam et hederas illico mori,die away, perish,: moriturque ad sibila campus,.—Of fire: flammas vidi nullo concutiente mori,die out, go out,; of comets: donec in exiguum moriens vanesceret ignem,: unguenta moriuntur,lose their strength,.—To end, close: dies quidem jam ad umbilicum est dimidiatus mortuus,.—Comic.: vae illis virgis miseris, quae hodie in tergo morientur meo,will find their death, be destroyed, broken,: ut iste interpositus sermo deliciarum desidiaeque moreretur,: ne suavissimi hominis memoria moreretur,: cum multa cotidie ab antiquis ficta moriantur,fall into disuse, become obsolete,: gratia,. —Esp. (in eccl. Lat.), of the loss of moral or spiritual vitality, to die, to lose virtue and divine guidance: in Adam omnes moriuntur,: confirma cetera quae moritura erant,; cf. ; .—Hence, mŏrtŭus, a, um, P. a., dead (class.).
Adj.
Lit.: sanguine tauri poto mortuus concidit,.—Prov.: mortuum esse alicui,to be dead to one, to wish to have nothing further to do with him,.—
Transf.
Of persons, faint, overwhelmed: cum tu, quod tibi succederetur, exsanguis et mortuus concidisti,.—
Of things concr. and abstr., dead, decayed, withered, passed away, etc.: lacerti,: flores,: et antiquae leges,: plausus,: mortuā re verba nunc facis. Stultus es, rem actam agis,dead, done with,.—
Mare mortuum.
The North Sea of Europe, .—
The Dead Sea of Judea, .—
Subst.: mŏrtŭus, i, m., a dead person, dead man: mortuum in domum inferre,: a mortuis excitare,to awake from the dead,: amandare aliquem infra mortuos,even below the dead,: ut multis mortuus unus sufficeret,: ossa mortuorum,.—Prov.: mortuo verba facere, to talk to a dead man, i. e. in vain, ; .—Esp. (eccl. Lat.), dead, without spiritual life: nomen habes quod vivas et mortuus es,: fides sine operibus mortua est,; cf. ; .—Also, dead to any thing, not alive to it, not open to its influence, etc.: peccato,: peccatis, Pet. 2, 24: legi,; cf.: mortui cum Christo ab elementis hujus mundi,: mortui estis, et vita vestra est abscondita cum Christo in Deo,.

la:noun:morum.html:
mōrum, i, n., = μῶρον and μόρον,
a mulberry; a blackberry: nigra mora,; cf. : in duris haerentia mora rubetis,; cf. .

la:noun:morus.html:
mōrus, i, f., = μῶρα or μορέα,
a mulberry-tree: arbor ibi, niveis uberrima pomis, Ardua morus erat,; cf. .

la:verb:morio.gloss: to die, be slain, fall (in battle), perish
senses: alternative form of morior (“to die”) (attested from the fourth century CE.)
la:verb:morio.html:
mōrĭo, ōnis, m., = μωρός,
an arrant fool (post-Aug.): quidam tantae sunt fatuitatis, ut non multum a pecoribus differant: quos moriones vulgo vocant,; ; ; in lemm.—
Transf., a monster, deformed person, .

la:adj:mortalis.html:
mortālis, e, adj.
mors
,
subject to death, liable to die, mortal (class.).
Lit.: quid in iis mortale et caducum, quid divinum aeternumque sit,: animal,.—
Transf.
Human, mortal: mucro,of human workmanship,: condicio vitae,: opera,: acta,: mortalin' decuit violari vulnere divum?from the hand of a mortal,: haud tibi vultus Mortalis,: nec mortale sonans,like a human voice,: si mortalis idem nemo sciat,.—Comp.: aliquid ipso homine mortalius,more perishable,.—Hence, subst.: mortālis, is, comm., a man, mortal, human being (in sing. mostly ante-class.): lepidus ecastor mortalis est Strabax,: edepol, mortalis malos,; ; : ego, quantum mortalis deum possum, te ac tua vestigia sequar,.—Usually pīur.: mortales, like the Gr. θνητοί, mortals, men, mankind: quod ad immortales attinet haec: deinceps quod ad mortales attinet, videamus, Müll.: est locus Hesperiam quam mortales perhibebant, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 23 Vahl.); cf.: omnes mortales sese laudarier optant, id. ap. (Ann. v. 551 Vahl.): omnes mortales hunc aiebant Calliclem vivere, etc.,: diu magnum inter mortales certamen fuit, etc.,: omnes mortales omnium generum, aetatum, ordinum,: defendo multos mortales,: plus debuisse fortunae, quam solus omnium mortalium in potestate habuit (Alexander),.—mortālĭa, ĭum, n., human affairs, ; .—
Temporary, transient (opp. immortalis, imperishable, eternal; v. immortalis): neque me vero paenitet, mortales inimicitias, sempiternas amicitias habere,; .— Hence, adv.: mortālĭter, mortally, in the manner of mortals (eccl. Lat.): mortaliter vivere,.

la:noun:mora.gloss: a duration of time before an event takes place, delay
senses: a duration of time before an event takes place, delay
a delay in the performance of an action, putting off
la:noun:mora.html:
mŏra, ae, f.
Sanscr. smar, remember; Gr. root μερ-, μαρ-; μέρμηρα, μέριμνα, care; μάρτυρ, witness; cf. memor, memoria; perh. μέλλειν
,
a delay.
Lit.
In gen.: tarditas sententiarum, moraque rerum,: mora et sustentatio,: mora aut tergiversatio,: moram rei alicui inferre,to delay, put off, defer, hinder,: moram ad insequendum intulit,: afferre,: facere delectui,: facere dimicandi,: facere creditoribus,to put off payment,: moras nectere,: offerre,: obicere,: trahere,to delay,: moliri,to cause delay,: producere malo alicui,to defer,: tibi moram dictis creas,: rumpere,: pellere,: corripere,: removere,to make haste, not to delay,: moram interponere,to interpose delay,: habeo paululum morae, dum, etc., Cass. ap. : Caesar nihil in morā habuit, quominus perveniret,delayed not,: saltus Castulonensis nequaquam tantā in morā est, does not hinder, Asin. Pall. ap. : nec mora ulla est, quin eam uxorem ducam,I will without delay,; so freq. in the poets: nec (haud) mora, ; ; ; : ne in morā illi sis,hinder, keep waiting,: per me nulla est mora,there is no delay on my part,: in me mora non erit ulla,; : nulla igitur mora per Novium ... quin, etc., it is no fault of Novius, etc., : nam si alia memorem, mora est,it will detain us too long,: inter

moras consul mittit senatum, in the meantime, meanwhile, : inter aliquas moras,; : sine mora, without delay, at once: quod ego, ut debui, sine mora feci,, : moram certaminis hosti exemit,i. e. hastened it on,.—

In partic., of speech, a stopping or pause: morae, respirationesque,: oratio non ictu magis quam morā imprimitur,. —
Transf.
Any thing that retards or delays, a hinderance: ne morae illi sim,: ne morae meis nuptiis egomet siem (al. mora),hinder,: hoc mihi morae est,: restituendae Romanis Capuae mora atque impedimentum es,: Abas pugnae nodusque moraque,: loricaeque moras et pectus perforat ingens,; cf. .—
Mora temporis, a space of time, : an tibi notitiam mora temporis eripit horum?: moram temporis quaerere dum Hannibal in Africam traiceret,; so, temporaria,.

la:noun:morbus.gloss: a disease, illness, malady, sickness, disorder, distemper, ailment
senses: a disease, illness, malady, sickness, disorder, distemper, ailment
la:noun:morbus.html:
morbus, i, m.
Sanscr. mar-, die; Gr. βροτός (for μροτός), μαραίνω; cf. morior, marceo
,
a sickness, disease, disorder, distemper, ailment, illness, malady, of body or mind (class.).
Corporeal: morbum appellant totius corporis corruptionem: aegrotationem morbum cum imbecillitate: vitium cum partes corporis inter se dissident: ex quo pravitas membrorum, distortio, deformitas,: morbus est habitus cujusque corporis contra naturam, qui usum ejus facit deteriorem, Labeo ap. : morbi aegrotationesque,: aeger morbo gravi,: in morbo esse,to be sick,: morbo affectum esse,: corporis gravioribus morbis vitae jucunditas impeditur,: animi valentes morbo tentari non possunt, corpora possunt,: affligi,: urgeri,: tabescere,: languere,: conflictari,: in morbum cadere,to fall sick,: incidere,: delabi,: morbum nancisci,: morbo consumi,: perire,: mori,: absumi,: confici,: opprimi,: homo aeger morbo gravi,: ex morbo convalescere,to recover,: a morbo valere,: morbum depellere,: levare,to alleviate, relieve,: amplior fit,becomes more violent,: adgravescit,: ingravescit,: comitialis or major,epilepsy,: regius,the jaundice,: in morbo consumat, a form of imprecation, may he spend it (the money) in sickness, .—
Mental.
Disease, a fault, vice, etc.: animi morbi sunt cupiditates immensae, et inanes, divitiarum, etc., : morbum et insaniam,: nomen insaniae significat mentis aegrotationem et morbum,: hic morbus qui est in re publicā, ingravescet,: ut, si qui aegrotet, quo morbo Barrus,: maxima pars hominum morbo jactatur eodem,: qui vultu morbum incessuque fatetur,.—
Grief, sorrow, distress: quod mulier facere incepit, nisi id efficere perpetrat, Id illi morbo, id illi senio est,affliction, distress,; cf.: salvere me jubes, quoi tu abiens offers morbum?.—
Trop., of trees, plants, etc.: infestantur namque et arbores morbis,a disease,—
Morbus, personified as a deity, the son of Erebus and Nox, ; Hyg. Fab. praef.; ; cf. ; .

senses: sharpness of flavor, sharp taste, pungency
jaw, tooth, fang, fluke (of an anchor)
la:noun:morsus.html:
morsus, ūs, m.
mordeo
,
a biting, a bite.
Lit.: contra avium minorum morsus munitur vallo aristarum. : serpentis,: morsu apprehendere,to bite,: morsibus insequi,: morsu appetere,: nec tu mensarum morsus horresce futuros,the eating,: mucida frusta farinae ... non admittentia morsum,: vertere morsus Exiguam in Cererem penuria adegit edendi,their bites, their teeth,, 112

; so, zonam morsu tenere,by the teeth,.—

Transf.
A catching hold; and, concr., that which takes hold, a catch (of a buckle, etc.; poet.): quā fibulā morsus Loricae crebro laxata resolverat ictu,: roboris,i. e. the cleft of the tree which held fast the javelin,: patulis agitatos morsibus ignes spirent,.—
Sharpness of flavor, sharp taste, pungency: nec cibus ipse juvat morsu fraudatus aceti,: marinus,acrid quality,: et scabros nigrae morsu rubiginis enses,i. e. a corroding, consuming,.—
Trop., a bite, sting, pain, vexation, etc.: (carmina) odio obscuro morsuque venenare,a malicious attack,: perpetui curarum morsus,gnawings, pains,: doloris,a bite, sting,: libertatis intermissae,: dubiā morsus famae depellere pugnā,.

senses: to bite into, take hold of, press or cut into
la:verb:mordeo.html:
mordĕo, mŏmordi (archaic memordi;
v.in the foll.), morsum, 2, v. a.
root smard-; Sanscr. mard-, bite; Gr. σμερδνός, σμερδαλέος; (cf. Engl. smart)
, to bite, to bite into (class.).
Lit.: si me canis memorderit, Enn. ap. (Sat. v. 36 Vahl.): canes mordere possunt,: mordens pulex,biting,: (serpens) fixum hastile momordit,bit into,: mordeat ante aliquis quidquid, etc.,taste,: terram, to bite the ground, bite the dust, of expiring warriors writhing on the ground: procubuit moriens et humum semel ore momordit,; .—Part. as subst.: morsi a rabioso cane,: laneaque aridulis haerebant morsa labellis,.—
In partic., to eat, devour, consume (poet.): tunicatum cum sale mordens Caepe,: ostrea,: sordes farris mordere canini,.—
Transf.
To bite into, take fast hold of, catch fast; to press or cut into (poet.): laterum juncturas fibula mordet,takes hold of, clasps,: mordebat fibula vestem,: id quod a lino mordetur,where the thread presses in,: locus (corporis), qui mucronem (teli) momordit,: arbor mordet humum,takes hold of the ground, is rooted in the ground,.—Hence, poet., of a river: non rura quae Liris quieta Mordet aqua, cuts or penetrates into, .—
To nip, bite, sting: matutina parum cautos jam frigora mordent,nips, attacks,: oleamque momorderit

aestus, : mordeat et tenerum fortior aura nemus,: radix gustu acri mordet,bites, hurts,: linguam,: oculos,: urtica foliis non mordentibus,stinging, burning,.—

Trop., to bite, sting, pain, hurt (syn.: pungo, stimulo, remordeo; class.): invidere omnes mihi, Mordere clanculum,bit, stung,: morderi dictis,: jocus mordens,a biting jest,: mordear opprobriis falsis,shall I be stung, vexed,: par pari referto, quod eam mordeat,to vex, mortify,: valde me momorderunt epistolae tuae,: scribis, morderi te interdum, quod non simul sis,that it grieves you, affects you,: dolore occulto morderi,to be attacked, tormented,: nec qui detrectat praesentia, Livor iniquo Ullum de nostris dente momordit opus,detracted,; cf. : morderi conscientiā,to feel the sting of conscience,: hunc mordebit objurgatio,.—
To seize fast, hold firmly in the mind (cf. mordicus, II.): hoc tene, hoc morde,. —
To squander, dissipate: de integro patrimonio meo centum milia nummūm memordi, Laber. ap. (Com. Rel. v. 50 Rib.).

la:verb:moror.gloss: to linger, loiter, spend time with
senses: to linger, loiter, spend time with
to impede, detain, cause to wait, hinder, hold back, stay
la:verb:moror.html:
mŏror, ātus, 1,
v. dep. n. and a. [mora].
Neutr., to delay, tarry, stay, wait, remain, linger, loiter (syn.: cesso, cunctor, haesito; class.); eamus ergo ad cenam: quid stas? Thr. Ubi vis: non moror,i. e. I have no objection,: Lucceius narravit, Brutum valde morari, non tergiversantem, sed exspectantem, si qui forte casus, etc.,: quid moror?: quid multis moror?why do I linger long? why make a long story of it?: ne multis morer,to be brief, in short,: paulum morandum in his intervallis,: quod adhuc Brundisii moratus es,have tarried, remained,: in provinciā,: haud multa moratus,i. e. without delaying long,: nec plura moratus,without tarrying any longer,: rosa quo locorum Sera moretur,may linger, may be,: Corycia semper qui puppe moraris,.—With cum: ubi, et cum quibus moreris,stay, reside,.—With quin: nec morati sunt quin decurrerent ad castra,.—In the part. perf. subst.: ad sexcentos moratorum in citeriore ripā cepit,; ; cf.: ad duo milia aut moratorum aut palantium per agros interfecta,; v. Drakenb. ad h. 1.—
Act., to delay, retard, detain, cause to wait, hinder: ne affinem morer, Quin, etc.,delay,: argentum non morabor quin feras,: morari ac sustinere impetum hostium,: conanti dexteram manum,: eum,: iter,: naves,: morari ab itinere proposito hostem,: morantur pauci Ridiculum et fugientem ex urbe pudorem,.—
To fix the attention of, to delight, amuse, entertain: morata recte Fabula Valdius oblectat, populum meliusque moratur, Quam, etc., delays, i. e. entertains, : carmina, quae possint oculos auresque morari Caesaris,arrest,: tardior stilus cogitationem moratur,: profecto non plus biduum aut—Ph. Aut? nihil moror, I will wait no longer, will bear no delay, : egomet convivas moror,keep them waiting,.—
In partic.: nihil morari aliquem, not to detain a person, to let him go, to dismiss. Thus the consul said when he dismissed the Senate: Nihil amplius vos moramur,I will detain you no longer, you are dismissed,. This is the customary formula for abandoning an accusation and dismissing an accused person: C. Sempronium nihil moror,i. e. I withdraw my accusation against,: cum se nihil morari magistrum equitum pronuntiasset,: negavit, se Gracchum morari,.—Hence,
Trop.: nihil morari (with acc., an object-clause, or quo minus), to let a thing go, i. e. not to value or regard, to care nothing about it, to have nothing to say against it, etc.: nam vina nihil moror illius orae,care nothing for it, am not fond of it,: officium,: nec dona moror,: nil ego istos moror faeceos mores, Brix ad loc.—With object-clauses: alieno uti nihil moror,I do not want to,: nihil moror, eos salvos esse, et ire quo jubetis, am not opposed to it, have nothing to say against it, Ant. ap. : nil moror eum tibi esse amicum,.— With quominus: nihil ego quidem moror, quominus decemviratu abeam,I do not hesitate to, I will immediately,. —Hence, * mŏrātē, adv., lingeringly, slowly: moratius,.!*?
Act. collat. form mŏro, āre: quid moras? Naev. ap. P.: morares Enn. ib.: moraret, Pac. ib. (cf. Vahl.; Trag. Rel. p. 82 Rib.; Com. Rel. p. 16 ib.).—
Pass. impers.: ita diu, ut plus biennium in his tricis moretur, be spent, lost, Cael. ap. .

la:noun:mors.html:
mors, tis, f.
root mor, v. morior
(dat. morte, Varr. ap. ),
death in every form, natural or violent (syn.: letum, nex).
Lit.: omnium rerum mors est extremum,: mors ultima linea rerum est,: mortem sibi consciscere,to kill one's self,: obire,to die,; Plaut Aul. prol. 15: nam necessest me ... cras mortem exequi,: certae occumbere morti,to submit to,: aliquem ad mortem dare,to put to death, kill,: morti,: aliquem morte multare,; so, per vim,: morte multatus,; ; ; : morte punire,; ; : mortis poena,: morti addici,: omne humanum genus morte damnatum est,: Antonius civium suorum vitae sedebat mortisque arbiter,: vitae et mortis habere potestatem,: illata per scelus,assassination,: ad mortem se offerre pro patriā,: afferre, Serv. ap. : multare aliquem usque ad mortem,: morte cadere,: morte acerbissimā affici, Serv. ap. : multare,: ad mortem duci,: cui legatio ipsa morti fuisset,brought death,: imperfecta,blindness,: morte suā mori, to die a natural death: bella res est, mori suā morte,: mors suprema,; : mortis fine, 2, 7: quae rapit ultima mors est, Lucil. ap. : proximus morti = moriens, , 22, 8; ; cf.: morti vicinus,; Hier. in Joel, 1, 13 al.; cf.: cui, mors cum appropinquet,: cujus aetati mors propior erat,: adpropinquante morte,: ut prorogetur tibi dies mortis,: circa mortis diem,: mansurum est vitium usque ad diem mortis,—Poet.: mors sola fatetur quantula sint hominum corpuscula,. —In plur.: mortes, when several persons are spoken of: praeclarae mortes sunt imperatoriae,; so : meorum,: perdere mortes,to throw away lives, to die in vain,: hinc subitae mortes,.—Also of different forms or modes of death: omnīs per mortīs,; cf.: omni imagine mortium,; .—Rarely of an abstract thing: fere rerum omnium oblivio morsque memoriae,death, total loss,.—
Personified.
Mors, a goddess, the daughter of Erebus and Nox, ; ; Hyg. Fab. praef.—
